newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Daimler uses new law to cut sick pay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Daimler uses new law to cut sick pay.

text.p: Germany's largest industrial giant, Daimler-Benz, on Tuesday stepped to the forefront in implementing controversial new legislation to cut sick pay for employees to 80 percent from October 1.

Unions and some leading politicians said companies like Daimler have no right to make such a cutback, saying the bill passed by parliament earlier this month was not meant to apply to existing contracts, only future ones.

But Daimler and other industrial leaders have taken a sharply different view and intend to use the legislation, part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Programme for More Jobs and Growth, to reopen talks with unions about how to cut costs.
"Wage contracts are not against this," Daimler said in a statement. "They are built on a legal basis which was changed as a result of this new law."

Union leaders are certain to react strongly to Daimler's decision, which could encourage other leading German firms to follow suit, leading to wholesale attempts to rewrite employee contracts concerning sick pay.

Daimler, which links the cutbacks with its ability to remain competitive in international markets, said it will now negotiate with its union on reducing the sick pay package, but would not say what would happen if no agreement was reached.
Earlier in the day a worried Kohl called on employers and unions to avoid escalating the fight over sick pay and said the two should resolve their differences in negotiations.

The sick pay law, introduced earlier this month, allows employers to pay 80 percent of wages on days when employees are off sick rather than the previous 100 percent. Sick pay in Germany currently totals 60 billion marks ($40 billion) a year.
Some employers have already cancelled contracts and said they aim to move immediately to reduce sick pay.
At the centre of the debate is the issue of whether the government's sick pay laws are meant to apply to existing contracts or only future ones.
German Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, along with Kohl, has so far sided with labour to some extent, warning employers who hope to reduce sick pay to abide by existing contracts until they expire.
But Hans Peter Stihl, president of the German Federation of Chambers of Commerce, said employers now had a firm legal basis to cut sick pay.

"The current contract regulations are sufficient to implement the cuts in sick pay," Stihl told a German newspaper over the weekend. Unions will probably seek court rulings, which could drag the matter out, he said.

Faced with huge cutbacks in benefits, labour is preparing to take industrial action. The IG Metall union has called for labour action on October 10 to protest against moves by companies to cut sick pay.
"We are not looking to strike, but we will strike if forced to," said IG Metall chairman Klaus Zwickel at the weekend. ($1=1.5124 Mark)
